x.A: Fargate with load testing and rightsizing helps cost, but all tasks run on regular Fargate pricing, so it doesn't use the lower-cost Spot capacity for bursts.
x.B: Regular Fargate capacity handles the steady state, which must be reliable 24/7, and Fargate Spot (a discount for interruptible capacity) handles short bursts of traffic cheaply. This keeps the workload highly available and cost-effective.
x.C: Using Fargate Spot for the steady state means tasks that can be interrupted would serve the baseline traffic, risking availability.
x.D: Compute Optimizer rightsizing is useful but doesn't use Spot pricing, so it costs more than the mixed approach.

x.A: Config rules evaluate resource configuration and don't detect DDoS attacks, and there's no proactive support.
x.B: WAF rules can block some floods, but WAF isn't a DDoS protection service with proactive engagement from AWS experts.
x.C: GuardDuty detects threats and doesn't take automated preventative actions against DDoS attacks.
x.D: Shield Advanced provides managed DDoS detection and mitigation, with proactive engagement from the Shield Response Team. Adding the ALB and Route 53 hosted zones as protected resources covers the application.

x.A: AWS WAF can't be associated with a Network Load Balancer, because it works with ALBs, API Gateway, and CloudFront.
x.B: An NLB can have a security group. Recreating the NLB with a security group that allows only trusted IP addresses blocks unauthorized access with minimal architectural change.
x.C: A second NLB with an allow list adds infrastructure, and an NLB without a security group can't filter by IP.
x.D: Shield Advanced protects against DDoS attacks, not against unauthorized access attempts.

x.A: A resource policy on the SNS topic that allows the Lambda function to publish gives the function permission to publish to the topic.
x.B: Using the AWS managed key instead of a customer managed key doesn't help with the permissions and goes against the requirement to use customer managed keys.
x.C: The KMS key policy must allow the principals (the Lambda function's role) to use the key so that they can publish to the encrypted topic.
x.D: The topic's resource policy allows principals to publish, and the function's ARN isn't the right principal. The function's role is used.
x.E: API Gateway isn't used to control Lambda access to an SNS topic, and it adds a needless layer.
x.F: The Lambda execution role needs IAM permissions to use the customer managed KMS key, such as kms:GenerateDataKey and kms:Decrypt, so the function can publish encrypted messages.

x.A: The web portal stays on EC2 On-Demand Instances in an Auto Scaling group, so there are no code changes and it stays available. A Lambda function runs the extract program on demand when a document is uploaded, so you pay only for use.
x.B: Spot Instances can be interrupted, and the portal needs 100% uptime.
x.C: A Savings Plan for both the portal and the extract program means paying for the extract program all the time, even though it runs only occasionally.
x.D: Moving the web portal to S3, API Gateway, and Lambda needs the portal to be rewritten, which involves code changes the company doesn't want.

x.A: A resource policy on the Lambda function that allows SNS to invoke it gives the SNS topic in the other account permission to call the function.
x.B: An SQS queue buffering messages adds an extra component that isn't needed for the function to be invoked.
x.C: The SNS topic's policy must allow the Lambda function in the other account to subscribe to the topic, so the topic can deliver messages to it.
x.D: EventBridge can't capture SNS topic notifications this way, and it adds a component.
x.E: Storing metrics in S3 for Athena doesn't invoke the function when metrics are reported.

x.A: A transit gateway connects networks and doesn't manage pod subnet configuration in EKS.
x.B: Direct Connect connects on-premises networks to AWS and doesn't set up custom subnets for pods.
x.C: The Amazon VPC CNI plugin supports custom networking, so pods can use specific subnets in the VPC, and pods communicate securely using VPC networking.
x.D: Network policies and anti-affinity rules control pod traffic and placement, not which VPC subnets the pods use.

x.A: Modifying the DB instance to Multi-AZ creates a standby in another AZ with automatic failover, with one change and little effort.
x.B: Migrating to DynamoDB is a different database model, so it needs a rewrite and a heterogeneous migration.
x.C: Creating a new Multi-AZ instance and restoring a snapshot means downtime and manual steps.
x.D: RDS can't be placed in an Auto Scaling group, and DNS simple routing doesn't replicate data.

x.A: FSx for NetApp ONTAP supports NFS and SMB on the same data (multi-protocol access), is managed, and a Multi-AZ deployment gives redundancy at the AZ level.
x.B: Two EC2 instances, one per protocol, are self-managed and the data wouldn't be shared between protocols.
x.C: FSx for Lustre provides POSIX access, not NFS in the sense required, and it doesn't share data with the SMB file system.
x.D: An S3 File Gateway can serve SMB and NFS but runs as a gateway on premises, and sharing between protocols isn't its design, and the data isn't in a file system.

x.A: A second instance in another Region with failover routing is a standby, not a scalable solution, and a Region is more than needed.
x.B: An Auto Scaling group in private subnets across multiple AZs behind an ALB makes the application scalable and highly available.
x.C: Aurora MySQL with a primary and a reader instance in separate AZs provides high availability and lowers read latency with a reader endpoint.
x.D: Auto Scaling groups can't span multiple Regions.
x.E: Cross-Region read replicas aren't needed to lower read latency in one Region and cost more.

x.A: Lambda@Edge is for running code at CloudFront edge locations, and creating security headers isn't how sensitive information is stored.
x.B: A Lambda layer that retrieves the sensitive information lets thousands of functions share the same code to fetch the secrets instead of duplicating it in each function.
x.C: Secrets Manager stores the sensitive information securely and rotates it automatically, which meets the requirement with little work.
x.D: Parameter Store has no native automatic rotation.
x.E: A Lambda consumer with dedicated throughput doesn't store or rotate secrets, and environment variables for thousands of functions would be hard to manage.

x.A: A Cost and Usage Report is raw cost data and doesn't contain cost recommendations.
x.B: CloudWatch billing alerts notify about spending thresholds and don't recommend optimizations.
x.C: Compute Optimizer gives recommendations for EC2 instances, Auto Scaling groups, and EBS volumes in one place, with the least effort.
x.D: Compute Optimizer already covers Auto Scaling groups and EBS volumes, so the extra report isn't needed.

x.A: S3 via API calls needs application changes and isn't a shared file system, and S3 traffic isn't kept inside the VPC without an endpoint.
x.B: S3 can't be mounted as a high-performance volume natively on EC2 instances.
x.C: An EBS volume attaches to a single instance in one AZ (apart from limited Multi-Attach), so it can't be shared across AZs.
x.D: EFS is a shared file system that instances across multiple AZs mount at the same time. Mount targets are inside the VPC, so the data stays in the VPC, and it performs well.

x.A: Deleting the read replica removes the capacity the reporting tool uses, and the reports would then load the primary, whose CPU is already 60%.
x.B: The replica runs at only 25% CPU, so a smaller replica still serves reports and saves cost. The primary at a steady 60% stays as it is, which leaves room for growth.
x.C: A larger replica would waste money since the replica CPU is at 25%, and shrinking the primary that's at 60% could cause overload.
x.D: Deleting the replica puts the reporting load on the primary, and increasing the primary size would cost more.

x.A: On-Demand pricing for RDS costs more than reserved pricing for a long-running database.
x.B: A 1 year No Upfront term gives a smaller discount than longer terms and upfront payment options.
x.C: A 1 year Partial Upfront option saves less than a 3 year All Upfront commitment for workloads that run long term.
x.D: A 3 year All Upfront term gives the largest discount for both RDS Reserved Instances and EC2 Instance Savings Plans, so it's the most cost-effective for long-running workloads.

x.A: Attaching the policy to the node role gives every pod on the nodes the same permissions, which isn't granular access per service account.
x.B: Network policies control pod network traffic, not AWS API permissions.
x.C: Changing the EKS cluster's IAM role doesn't map permissions to each service account, and Kubernetes roles aren't IAM roles.
x.D: An IAM role with the needed permissions is annotated on the Kubernetes service account (by ARN), so pods using that service account get only those permissions.
x.E: The IAM role's trust policy must trust the cluster's OIDC identity provider, so service accounts can assume the role.

x.A: SSE-C needs the company to supply and manage its own keys, and CloudTrail can't track their rotation.
x.B: SSE-S3 keys are managed by S3, and key rotation isn't visible or trackable in CloudTrail.
x.C: SSE-KMS with the AWS managed key (aws/s3) is rotated automatically every year, key use and rotation are logged in CloudTrail, and AWS managed keys have no monthly key fee, so it costs the least.
x.D: A customer managed KMS key costs a monthly fee per key, so it's more expensive than the AWS managed key for this requirement.

x.A: AWS Budgets can't be used to download cost data by application like that, and a .csv lookup is manual.
x.B: Loading Cost and Usage Reports into RDS and running SQL queries costs more for the database and takes effort.
x.C: Tagging resources by application and activating the cost allocation tags lets Cost Explorer break down costs by application, with regular reports and no extra infrastructure.
x.D: Downloading bills and looking up the information is manual, and bills aren't broken down by tag unless allocation tags are activated.

x.A: Everything in a single AZ is a single point of failure, even if S3 versioning protects assets.
x.B: An Auto Scaling group across multiple AZs, a Multi-AZ RDS instance, and CloudFront for static assets make every tier resilient and highly available.
x.C: A single AZ for EC2 isn't resilient, and serving static assets from EC2 adds load to the instances.
x.D: Lambda for a web application that was built for EC2 needs a redesign, and EFS One Zone-IA is a single AZ, so it isn't resilient.

x.A: An NLB with an interface endpoint exposes a service privately, but it doesn't insert a security appliance transparently in the traffic path to inspect traffic.
x.B: An ALB sends HTTP and HTTPS traffic to targets, and can't send traffic across accounts directly to an appliance for inspection.
x.C: A Gateway Load Balancer in the networking account sends traffic to the security appliance, and GWLB endpoints in the application accounts route traffic to it transparently for inspection.
x.D: An interface endpoint can't send traffic directly to an appliance without a load balancer, and it doesn't inspect interactions.

x.A: An Aurora custom endpoint groups specific replicas (here, the three with different specs) and load balances connections across just those instances, so the department's reporting queries are distributed over them.
x.B: Cloning a cluster creates a separate cluster with its own cost and storage copy, which isn't needed.
x.C: Instance endpoints connect to one specific instance, so the queries wouldn't be distributed automatically.
x.D: The reader endpoint distributes across all replicas, not just the selected three.

x.A: Parameter Store has no built-in automatic rotation.
x.B: Secrets Manager stores the credentials securely and rotates the RDS for PostgreSQL credentials automatically. The Lambda function simply retrieves the secret.
x.C: An encrypted environment variable with a custom Lambda rotation function means building and maintaining rotation code.
x.D: KMS stores keys, not database credentials, and key rotation doesn't rotate a database password.

x.A: A Multi-AZ replication instance gives high availability, but it provisions fixed capacity, so it doesn't allocate only the needed capacity.
x.B: DMS Serverless automatically provisions, scales, and manages the replication capacity as the data volume changes, so only the capacity required is allocated.
x.C: A DMS replication instance isn't an EC2 instance you control with Auto Scaling.
x.D: DMS replication isn't provisioned through ECS and Fargate.

x.A: A Site-to-Site VPN connects networks and doesn't connect to a SaaS provider hosted on AWS privately in this manner.
x.B: A transit gateway routes between VPCs and networks in your control, and can't connect to a third-party provider's service.
x.C: This describes PrivateLink in a limited way, but it doesn't establish the private connection to the SaaS provider's service.
x.D: AWS PrivateLink creates a private interface endpoint in the application's VPC to the SaaS provider's endpoint service, so traffic stays on the AWS network with minimal public internet exposure.

x.A: Direct Connect isn't encrypted by default, so it doesn't meet the requirement to encrypt all traffic.
x.B: IAM policies control console and resource access and don't connect the networks or encrypt traffic.
x.C: Site-to-Site VPN (IPsec) encrypts all traffic at the network and session layers. Route table entries direct traffic, and security groups and network ACLs allow only required traffic from on premises.
x.D: A transit gateway connects networks, but by itself it doesn't provide encryption of traffic between on premises and the VPC without a VPN.
